title: Man called newspaper before fatal shooting near Sharbot Lake
article: The events that led to the fatal shooting of an Arden man by the Ontario Provincial Police last Thursday started with a call to an area newspaper.
The Frontenac News, an independent weekly, had fielded several calls over the past seven months from Bob Srigley.
Srigley, 45, had last called the Frontenac News office on Thursday afternoon at 4 pm.
He wished to speak to the editor, Jeff Green, about an incident with police that took place in November 2012, and that the News covered.
"I had done stories on him in the past. I didn't talk to him at that time," said Green, who was at home when Srigley called.

According to an article in the Frontenac News from late last week, Srigley declined the opportunity to call Green at home, followed by saying that he was going to get in his boat and set himself on fire.
The managing editor and receptionist who took the call then decided to call Green themselves.
"We decided to phone 911 because (Srigley) said he was considering suicide," Green said. "We figured that was our only option although we ... didn't know how he would respond."

According to a report from the OPP following the incident, officer from the Lanark Detachment "attended a rural residence on Arden Road" at around 5:29 pm on Thursday, July 25, shortly after the call from the Frontenac News.
Although the OPP have yet to release Srigley's name, Frontenac News has named him as the man involved. Green said he knew it was him as the details matched.
"During the interaction between OPP officers and a male at the residence, police firearms were discharged and the man was struck multiple times," the OPP report said.
Srigley underwent surgery at Kingston General Hospital. He died Sunday night.
The Ontario Special Investigations Unit (SIU) is now investigating the case.
Green said his first interaction with Srigley was in November 2012, when Srigley claimed "he'd been beaten up by police."
"His accusation was that it was an off-duty police officer that beat him up in November," Green said.
Srigley contacted the Frontenac News to talk about his situation and to seek help from the public, Green said.

As he was on Ontario Disability Support Program for a previous injury, Srigley didn't work. Because of injuries he said were sustained from the November altercation, he said he was unable to do certain tasks to prepare his trailer for the winter.
"Part of his circumstances were (that) he didn't have a lot of money, and he had issues getting his wood in for the winter," Green said.
The Frontenac News followed the case for some months, during which time it was brought to the OPP Complaints Commission.
"In March, the decision was made ... to close the investigation," Green, who wrote an article detailing the results, said.
This was the second of three articles Green would publish about Srigley. The third one was two weeks ago.
"He wanted people to know that he needed help," he said. "I think it worked originally, back in November, maybe in March, but I'm not sure how much help he received."
Green said Srigley, who lived alone, was a somewhat isolated individual and that he wasn't sure if he had family.
"He was pushing further investigation and he wanted people's support," he said.
The investigation by the Special Investigations Unit, into Srigley's death, is ongoing.
